newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia stocks, ringgit not seen setting new trend.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia stocks, ringgit not seen setting new trend.

text.p: Malaysian stocks are drawing value-seekers even as the ringgit faces overseas selling this week in what will likely be short-lived trends, analysts and fund managers said on Wednesday.
After a 6.8 percent tumble since curbs on property and stock lending were announced on March 28, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index staged a 2.47 percent rebound on Tuesday.
At midday on Wednesday, the index was up 0.34 percent to 1,166.23 points.
"We see no reason for investors to underweight positions during this consolidation," Jupiter Securities said in its morning research note on Wednesday. "There is still gold in the market."
Analysts noted that Malaysian stocks were trading at a price-to-earnings multiple of between 16 to 19 times compared with historical valuations of 20 to 21 times.

As for the ringgit, it has been hit by sales of the Malaysian unit against the Singapore dollar. Dealers said there was also talk a U.S. hedge fund was closing its outright three-month long ringgit position this week.

"The concern of the market is that the U.S. fund who had been previously buying up the ringgit-Sing cross may be inclined to take profits and appear to be doing so since last week," said Andy Tan, an economist at MMS International.
But he said his firm was not changing its forecast for the ringgit of 2.45/dollar at year-end. At 0600 GMT on Wednesday, the ringgit was at 2.5058/68 to a dollar.
Dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia, the country's central bank, intervened on Wednesday to stem the currency's fall at 2.5120 a dollar.
Referring to the stock market's rise over the past two days, Robert Coombe, executive director of Commerce Asset Fund Managers, said:
"I don't think there's any need to get excited. Nothing's changed, but maybe people are starting to realise they overreacted to the Bank Negara news and (interest rate) hike in the U.S."
Bank Negara announced at the end of March it was imposing stricter rules for bank loans on property and stock purchase financing.
It required banks and finance companies to trim their exposure to the property sector to 20 percent of total outstanding loans from the present 30 percent level.
The central bank also imposed new curbs on using shares as collateral to buy other stocks.
"This rebound will be short-term," said Ang Kok Heng, general manager at TA Asset Management, referring to the stock market's performance. "I don't think the market has stabilised."
But Ang said he still maintained his target for the Composite Index, a blue chip barometer, at 1,300 at the end of 1997.
